newsitem.title: USA: Lehman exits commodities OTC trading to cut costs.
newsitem.headline: Lehman exits commodities OTC trading to cut costs.

text.p: Lehman Brothers said Wednesday it is winding down its metals and energy over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives trading operations, completing an exit from commodities, because of poor returns.
This will result in the loss of about 35 front office and support jobs, with most concentrated in London, according to Lehman Brothers spokesman Bill Ahearn.

In a letter to clients, Chris Deuters, head of Lehman Brothers European Fixed Income division, said that the investment bank would stop writing new metals and energy OTC business as of the close of business on November 20. The bank will work with clients to close out or transfer existing positions, he said.
The latest move is part of a broader wind down of the bank's energy and commodities opeations as part of Lehman's efforts to boost its relatively poor return on equity.

Last year, Lehman pulled out of trading on the International Petroleum Exchange and moved the global headquarters for its energy derivatives trading from London to New York, though it remained one of the larger players in the energy derivatives market.
"It really takes away a lot of liquidity," said one market participant. "Lehman accounted for a lot of the swaps liquidity."
In October, Lehman closed its London gold trading desk, dropped out of most metals and U.S. natural gas trading.
"What we are looking to do is allocate our resources to businesses where we have a competitive edge and from time to time we'll go through this exercise," said Ahearn.

Though its return on equity improved in the first half of this year to around 11.5 percent, Lehman has been lagging other major Wall Street players where returns are between 15 and 20 percent. This has been reflected in its share price which trades below book value and Lehman has frequently been the subject of takeover talk.
